title: Redemption for Arch Manning and Sark? Texas stuns Ohio State with 20-point comeback
author: Ralph D. Russo
content:
AUSTIN, Texas — Arch Manning had his moment, Steve Sarkisian earned that elusive, validating victory against another super heavyweight program and Texas beat a top-ranked team at home for the first time in 76 years with a 21-point fourth-quarter rally.

Hollywood Smothers dove over the line from a yard out for a touchdown with 25 seconds left and the fourth-ranked Longhorns stunned No. 1 Ohio State 24-23 on Saturday night.

The Buckeyes led 23-3 heading into the fourth quarter, but Manning led three straight long touchdown drives to wipe out the deficit. The final one started with 4:16 left at the Texas 27-yard line after Ohio State missed a 45-yard field goal that could have all but clinched the Buckeyes third straight victory over the Longhorns.

Manning, who passed for 196 yards and a touchdown, hit Emmett Mosley on a slant for 19 yards that got Texas to first-and-goal at the 1 with 1:02 left in regulation. After two trunks up the middle gained nothing for Texas, Smothers, one of the Longhorns’ high-priced transfer portal additions, jumped over the top to give Texas its first lead.

Ohio State’s desperation drive ended with an interception by Graceson Littleton as time expired. The Longhorns rushed the field, and a few fans joined them, celebrating the first Texas victory at home against a No. 1 team since beating SMU in 1950.

Jeremiah Smith starred for Ohio State, with eight catches for 164 yards and a touchdown, but after an early third quarter field goal to go up 23-3, the Buckeyes couldn’t muster another point.

Here’s what we took away from the comeback:

For Texas, which started last season as preseason No. 1 but failed to reach the College Football Playoff after losing a season-opener at Ohio State, the victory marks a new mile-marker in its ascent under Sarkisian.

The sixth-year coach took the Longhorns to the CFP semifinals in 2024 and 2025, but three losses to Georgia and two to Ohio State since joining the SEC had led some to wonder if Sark had hit his ceiling.

For three quarters against the Buckeyes, that looked to be the case again.

Until three straight drives, with Manning leading the way, delivered the signature moment of both the quarterback’s and coach’s time at Texas so far.

Winning a game like this announces the Longhorns as a legitimate national championship contender. Sarkisian can stiff-arm the critics who have questioned his big-game performances in the past, at least for a little while. And Manning can silence some of his doubters as well for leading Texas out of that 20-point deficit.

For the last three seasons, Texas has been one of college football’s top programs, going 37-8 since the start of the 2024 season. But it hasn’t yet won the big one. Texas’ last national championship came in 2005. Notably, a close Week 2 win over Ohio State, 25-22 on Sept. 10, 2005, proved a catalyst in that season’s title run. — Ralph D. Russo and Sam Khan Jr.

When Manning made his debut as Texas’ full-time starter in 2025, the season-opening loss to Ohio State proved to be his toughest test. He struggled mightily and endured seemingly endless criticism in the aftermath, though he got a lot better as the year progressed and finished the season strong.

The rematch against the Buckeyes represented a chance for redemption, and for a while, it didn’t seem he would get it. The turnovers and drops by his teammates in the first three quarters made his job that much harder. Manning also missed some throws and made some mistakes of his own and the offense, as a whole, look disjointed.

But the fourth quarter belonged to Manning. The Longhorns’ offensive line deserves credit, because it gave him time when Texas sped up the tempo to get back into the game. But Manning was accurate, decisive and didn’t needlessly put the ball in harm’s way while leading three consecutive touchdown drives.

People ask whether the hype surrounding Manning is solely due to his name. The numbers weren’t eye-popping, but his poise under pressure and ability to lead Texas back from a 20-point deficit against the No. 1 team in the nation should put some of those questions to rest, because his performance did plenty of the talking for him. — Khan

Texas might’ve made the Playoff last year if it played a cupcake instead of Ohio State, which might have meant it finished 10-2 (the Longhorns did beat two-loss CFP team Oklahoma, after all). But two weeks into 2026, this game reminded us of the value of high-profile, nonconference games.

Texas’ Playoff hopes have room for error now. Even with a demanding SEC schedule still to come — games against No. 18 Tennessee, No. 11 Oklahoma, No. 9 Ole Miss, No. 8 LSU and No. 10 Texas A&M — the Longhorns can lose a game or two and still make the field.

That is why more teams added marquee nonconference games when it was clear the CFP was going to expand to 12. It helps attendance and the upside is massive.

Sarkisian confirmed two weeks ago that next year’s Michigan game is on, which is a return trip to Austin for the 2024 game. But Sarkisian has been less committed to Texas’ games against Notre Dame in 2028 and 2029. Even athletic director Chris Del Conte, who has stood stronger behind the marquee matchups, said earlier this month he wasn’t fully sure if the Longhorns would stick with it.

Saturday night’s win against Ohio State was a reminder of why these games need to keep happening.

And besides, CFP leaders last week triggered a 30-day window to begin TV negotiations with ESPN. It was not a commitment to expansion to 24 teams in 2027, but it was one step closer. — Chris Vannini

For most of the first three quarters, Texas’ supposed high-powered offense looked like all sizzle, no steak.

Then in the fourth quarter, somehow, the Longhorns resembled the unit they were supposed to be. Manning got into rhythm. The offensive line gave him all the time in the world. And the Longhorns’ skill position players stopped making self-inflicted mistakes. And just like that, Texas an embarrassing first three quarters into a seminal victory.

After compiling only 186 yards through the first three quarters, Texas chewed up 150 in the final stanza, with Manning going 8-for-11 passing for 83 of those yards.

Texas righted a lot of wrongs in the final quarter. The Longhorns turned the ball over twice in their first five plays of the game, first with a Raleek Brown fumble, next when Cam Coleman dropped what would have been a 50-yard completion and instead watched it turn into an interception when it bounced out of his hands and into those of Jaylen McClain. Ryan Wingo, who caught Texas’ first touchdown of the game early in the fourth quarter, dropped what would have been a wide-open touchdown pass from Manning midway through the second quarter.

Texas failed on a fourth-and-1 late in the first half, opening an opportunity for Ohio State to score a touchdown and extend its lead to 20-3 just before the half. And Manning missed some throws throughout the night that he would have liked to have had back.

Everything that could have gone wrong in the first half, for the most part, did for Texas. And the Longhorns will have to correct some of those issues, because their schedule is too tough to sleepwalk through like that.

But Texas showed its resilience and showed that it can be tested and survive it. And all the money they spent on their transfers, including Coleman, Smothers and Brown, was well spent Saturday. — Khan

This story will be updated. More to come.
